title: Design a coral: for heat, for shape, or for the reef
subtitle: The question is 'could you engineer a coral' — and the first job is to refuse it, because it bundles four different animals. A THERMALLY TOLERANT colony, a colony of a CHOSEN MORPHOLOGY (which decides flow, light capture, nursery habitat and what a storm breaks), a colony that SETTLES AND SURVIVES where you put it, and a HOLOBIONT engineered through its symbiont or microbiome rather than through the animal at all. These are different scales with different evidence, different costs and different irreversibility. Nothing below has been attempted here.
nothing_attempted: None of these routes has been attempted here.

scales.label: Molecular · sequence and regulation
scales.blurb: Enhancers, methylation and polygenic scores. The level at which coral is furthest behind: no coral enhancer has ever been validated, and the PubMed search for Acropora ATAC-seq returns zero against five for Nematostella run the same way.

scales.label: Gene · targeted edits in the animal
scales.blurb: CRISPR/Cas9 in Acropora millepora works, in the injected generation, and has produced exactly four published coral phenotypes. There is no stable transgenic or germline-edited coral line anywhere in the literature read here.

scales.label: Cell and tissue · calcification
scales.blurb: The calicoblastic epithelium raises pH and concentrates bicarbonate under the skeleton. One gene in that pathway has a loss-of-function coral phenotype; everything else is localisation, expression and inhibitor work.

scales.label: Symbiont · Symbiodiniaceae
scales.blurb: Change the alga, not the animal. The best-evidenced thermal route and the one with the clearest measured cost. Seven genera, a shuffling literature that disagrees with itself in a way that has been partly reconciled, and no genome-edited symbiont.

scales.label: Microbiome · bacteria, phage, antibiotics
scales.blurb: Beneficial Microorganisms for Corals. Striking tank results, one in-water heatwave trial, and inoculants that in every study read here disappear within weeks. The one microbial intervention with a real field record is an antibiotic for a disease whose pathogen is unknown.

scales.label: Colony · growth form and mechanics
scales.blurb: Branching, plating, massive. Decides flow, light capture, what a storm breaks and what fish live in it. Substantially plastic, steerable by environment without touching a gene, and the one scale with a published runnable model class.

scales.label: Population · breeding and gene flow
scales.blurb: Selective breeding, assisted gene flow, hybrids, cryobanking. The only family of routes with anything like a deployment programme behind it, and still no located instance of a bred coral on the Great Barrier Reef.

scales.label: Larval · settlement and recruitment
scales.blurb: Where restoration actually fails. Adults survive; recruits do not. Cues, devices, substrate, grazing and sediment, with first-year survival spread over more than tenfold across sites and thermal years.

scales.label: Ecological and regulatory · the reef, the law
scales.blurb: Siting, permits, scale and what the whole portfolio is for. A median restoration project covers 100 square metres. The arithmetic that follows from that is the honest frame for everything above.

outcome_classes.label: Settles and survives where you put it

outcome_classes_note: THE OUTCOME IS DECLARED PER ROUTE, as a field, not inferred from the text. An earlier version assigned it by running these regexes over each route's own prose and taking the first match, and it was wrong in about ten of forty-five cases in ways that all looked plausible: the HSF1 knockout came out as 'recruitment' because its phenotype is in larvae, the Durusdinium route came out as 'skeleton' because the cost it pays is calcification, and the flow-plasticity route came out as 'skeleton' because the sentence explaining it mentions skeleton already laid down. A pattern run over prose classifies the prose. The regexes are KEPT, but only as an audit: build_routes.py records where the declared outcome and the pattern disagree, and those disagreements are data about the writing, not corrections to the tag.

routes.title: Make the coral enhancer map that does not exist yet
routes.intervention: Generate ATAC-seq, ChIP-seq and Hi-C in Acropora and Stylophora, in larvae, juveniles and heat-stressed adults, and validate a handful of candidate enhancers with reporter constructs.
routes.predicted_phenotype: No coral. The product is the first map of which non-coding coral DNA is open and active, which is the thing every 'tune the regulation of gene X' proposal below silently assumes already exists.
routes.mechanism: Infrastructure. Nothing is perturbed.

evidence.cite: Scoped negative: PubMed query 'Acropora ATAC-seq' returns 0. The same query shape for Nematostella returns 5 (PMIDs 36396969, 34299075, 31693674, 29856957, 24642862). Searched: PubMed only, one query shape, genus Acropora only. NOT searched: Stylophora, Pocillopora, Porites, Montipora individually, bioRxiv, GEO, SRA, theses. So the claim is 'no peer-reviewed coral enhancer-validation paper found in PubMed', not 'none exists'.

Weizman et al. 2019, PLoS Genet 15:e1008397 — ATAC-seq in Nematostella; 259 active enhancers under light-dark and 333 under dark-dark. With Schwaiger below, this is the only validated cnidarian cis-regulatory dataset, so any 'edit coral enhancer X' proposal currently rests on borrowing its grammar — which is cis_regulatory_inference at best.

Schwaiger et al. 2014, Genome Res 24:639 — ChIP-seq of five chromatin marks in Nematostella; >5,000 enhancers, 75% of those tested validated in vivo. The positive control that makes the coral zero meaningful.

routes.evidence_transfer_label: an anemone or Nematostella, not a coral
routes.evidence_transfer_note: The only validated cnidarian enhancer map is in Nematostella, which is not a coral and does not calcify. The scoped negative that motivates the route is about Acropora, so the route is a proposal to REMOVE this transfer gap, not to rely on it.

routes.title: Reprogramme gene-body methylation to harden a colony
routes.intervention: Apply a conditioning regime, or a methylation-modifying treatment, intended to leave a durable epigenetic mark.
routes.predicted_phenotype: Unpredictable, and the two papers read here point opposite ways. This route is in the table because it is widely proposed, not because anyone has shown it does anything.
routes.mechanism: Disputed. Methylation may reduce transcriptional noise and shift with long-term stress, or may be unrelated to expression plasticity on physiological timescales.

evidence.cite: Liew et al. 2018, Sci Adv 4:eaar8028 — in Stylophora pistillata, methylation reduces spurious transcription; long-term pH stress shifted methylation in cell-cycle and body-size pathways, with larger cells and more porous skeletons. Read as an epigenetic component of acclimatisation BY THE AUTHORS.

Abbott, Loockerman & Matz 2024, Evol Appl 17:e13662 — 'Modifications to gene body methylation do not alter gene expression plasticity in a reef-building coral'; methylation change had negligible or no association with expression plasticity. DISAGREES with the above. The two use different species and different stressors and neither reports on the other, so this is unresolved rather than refuted.

routes.evidence_transfer_note: Liew et al. is Stylophora; Abbott et al.'s abstract names no species. The two also disagree, so the route rests on cross-genus transfer of a disputed effect.

routes.title: Knock out HSF1 — the calibration experiment, not a design
routes.intervention: Microinject Cas9 ribonucleoprotein and a guide against the heat-shock transcription factor HSF1 into fertilised Acropora millepora eggs.
routes.predicted_phenotype: Larvae that live normally at 27 degC and die rapidly at 34 degC, where wild-type and Cas9-only larvae showed no detectable mortality. This marks the floor of coral thermal tolerance. It does NOT give you a heat-tolerant coral and was never meant to.
routes.mechanism: HSF1 is necessary for the larval heat-shock response; removing it removes the response.
routes.reversibility: none in that animal; injected generation only, no line
routes.lethality_risk: high at heat, low at ambient

evidence.cite: Cleves et al. 2020, PNAS 117:28899 — >90% of HSF1 gene copies mutant; survived at 27 degC, died rapidly at 34 degC.
Tinoco et al. 2026, Nat Protoc 21:2851 — the protocol paper, which states this approach 'is currently the only way to perform gene editing in corals' and takes about 2 to 4 weeks.

routes.evidence_transfer_note: Target and evidence are the same species. One of only a handful of routes in this table for which that is true.

routes.title: Raise the baseline instead: engineer constitutive frontloading
routes.intervention: Edit the regulation of HSF1 targets — heat-shock proteins, antioxidant enzymes, apoptosis regulators — so they sit high before any heat arrives.
routes.predicted_phenotype: A coral that starts hot-ready, like the resilient Acropora hyacinthus colonies in which 60 such genes are already elevated at control temperature. The cost of carrying that expression constitutively is UNMEASURED, and is the obvious place a trade-off would hide.
routes.mechanism: Frontloading: constitutive expression means less to induce under stress.
routes.reversibility: heritable if germline, and no germline coral line exists

evidence.cite: Barshis et al. 2013, PNAS 110:1387 — resilient A. hyacinthus colonies had higher control-condition expression of 60 'frontloaded' genes. This is a CORRELATION between colonies, not a demonstration that those genes cause tolerance.

Palumbi et al. 2014, Science 344:895 — reciprocal transplant; acclimatisation and fixed effects contributed about equally, and acclimatisation reached in under two years what selection would take many generations to give.
Cleves et al. 2020 — the only targeted edit with a coral heat phenotype, and it is loss-of-function. Nothing shows that RAISING HSF1 activity raises tolerance.

routes.evidence_transfer_note: The frontloading correlation is in A. hyacinthus; the only causal edit is in A. millepora. Same genus, different species, and the two results are different KINDS of evidence.

routes.title: Edit SLC26A11 and lose the symbiosis
routes.intervention: CRISPR/Cas9 mutagenesis of the symbiosomal bicarbonate/sulfate transporter SLC26A11.
routes.predicted_phenotype: Reduced symbiosis. Reported in Aiptasia and, per the same abstract, in a reef-building coral. This is a route to UNDERSTANDING how the symbiosome is supplied, not a route to a better coral: its phenotype is the thing everything else is trying to protect.
routes.mechanism: The symbiosome membrane transporter supplies the alga; removing it breaks the supply. Lysosomal machinery was co-opted for this symbiosis.
routes.difficulty: low once the injection pipeline runs

evidence.cite: Maruyama et al. 2026, Cell 189:5640 — 'Co-option of lysosomal machinery shapes the evolution of the intracellular photosymbiosis supporting coral reefs'; CRISPR/Cas9 showed SLC26A11 'is required for symbiosis in Aiptasia and a reef-building coral'. The abstract does not say whether the Aiptasia mutants are germline lines or injected mosaics.

routes.evidence_transfer_label: an anemone or Nematostella, not a coral
routes.evidence_transfer_note: The abstract reports the requirement 'in Aiptasia and a reef-building coral' but does not name the coral, so the coral half cannot be placed.

routes.title: Get knockdown and knock-in working, in the coral that is easy first
routes.intervention: Build out shRNA knockdown, exogenous-mRNA overexpression and CRISPR knock-in in Astrangia poculata, then port the toolkit to a reef-builder.
routes.predicted_phenotype: No phenotype of interest. The product is the ability to turn a coral gene DOWN and to put a sequence IN, neither of which has been published in a reef-building coral.
routes.mechanism: Tool development. Astrangia is a hard coral, facultatively symbiotic, temperate and not reef-building, which is exactly why it is tractable and exactly why the transfer is not guaranteed.

evidence.cite: Warner et al. 2025, EvoDevo 16:6 — shRNA knockdown, overexpression from exogenous mRNA, and CRISPR knock-in in Astrangia poculata.

Scoped negative: PubMed 'Acropora knockdown' returns 0. 'Acropora CRISPR' returns 4 (29695630, 33168726, 37276409, 41772232). Searched with that one query shape; RNAi and morpholino literature under other terms was not searched.
Cleves et al. 2018, PNAS 115:5235 — the founding method: Cas9 RNP into fertilised A. millepora eggs targeting FGF1a, GFP and RFP, mutations in about 50% of individuals.

routes.evidence_transfer_label: a stony coral that does not build reefs
routes.evidence_transfer_note: Astrangia is a temperate, facultatively symbiotic, non-reef-building stony coral. That is exactly why it is tractable and exactly why the transfer is not guaranteed. The route is about MOVING the toolkit, so the gap is the point.

routes.title: Break the bicarbonate supply and watch the skeleton fail
routes.intervention: CRISPR mutation of SLC4-gamma in Acropora millepora zygotes.
routes.predicted_phenotype: Juvenile polyps with a defective skeleton, with defect severity tracking the mutation frequency within each animal. The cleanest genotype-to-skeleton link in the coral literature.
routes.mechanism: SLC4-gamma supplies concentrated bicarbonate to the extracellular calcifying medium under the calicoblastic epithelium. It arose by gene duplication at the origin of stony corals and is absent from their non-skeleton-forming relatives.

evidence.cite: Tinoco et al. 2023, PNAS 120:e2216144120 — 30 coral genomes and 15 outgroups; SLC4-gamma present throughout stony corals and not in non-skeleton-forming relatives; CRISPR mutants defective in skeleton formation with severity correlated to mutation frequency.

THE INVERSE IS UNTESTED. Raising SLC4-gamma — by exogenous mRNA or a stronger promoter — might give a faster skeleton, and nobody has tried it in a coral. A transport step that is NECESSARY is not thereby RATE-LIMITING, so this is a proposal, not a prediction. mRNA overexpression has been shown in Astrangia poculata (PMID 40380248), not in Acropora.
Zoccola et al. 2015, Sci Rep 5:9983 — eight SLC genes in Stylophora (five SLC4, three SLC26) with expression and immunostaining placing SLC4-gamma as the bicarbonate supplier.

routes.evidence_transfer_note: The CRISPR phenotype is in the target species; the Stylophora work is supporting expression and localisation only.

routes.title: The rest of the calcification machinery, where nothing has been tested genetically
routes.intervention: Genetically perturb STPCA, the secreted alpha carbonic anhydrase immunolocalised to the calicoblastic ectoderm.
routes.predicted_phenotype: Expected: reduced calcification. UNTESTED GENETICALLY in any coral. Every existing result on this enzyme is localisation, expression or in-vitro inhibitor chemistry, and inhibitors have off-target effects.
routes.mechanism: Carbonic anhydrase interconverts CO2 and bicarbonate at the calcifying interface; it is expressed about twofold higher in dark than in light.

evidence.cite: Skeletal organic matrix proteins — coral acid-rich proteins and galaxin — are abundant in the skeletal proteome and localised in both tissue and mineral, and NO knockdown or knockout of any of them has been published. Ramos-Silva et al. 2013, Mol Biol Evol, 'The skeletal proteome of the coral Acropora millepora'; listing only.
Drake et al. 2014, PNAS — immunolocalisation of skeletal matrix proteins in tissue and mineral of Stylophora pistillata. Listing only.

Calcium ATPase is inferred to drive the pH up-regulation from boron isotopes in cold-water corals, and no coral paper with a genetic test of it was found; a Stylophora Ca-ATPase inhibitor query returned 0. V-type H+-ATPase was NOT searched at all, so nothing is claimed about it.

Scoped negative: among every component in this pathway, ONLY SLC4-gamma has a gene-level necessity result in a coral. Searches: 'coral acid-rich protein skeletal organic matrix' (5 hits) and 'coral galaxin skeletal organic matrix' (5 hits), titles only, no full text. A null result here could also mean redundancy rather than irrelevance.

Moya et al. 2008, J Biol Chem 283:25475 — STPCA cloned from Stylophora pistillata, immunolocalised to the calicoblastic ectoderm, about twofold higher in dark than light. The authors note earlier tests of carbonic anhydrase in calcification were 'mainly by pharmacological approaches'.

routes.evidence_transfer_note: The calcium-ATPase inference comes from COLD-WATER, azooxanthellate corals — a different ocean, a different depth and no symbionts. That is the weakest link and it carries the pH-up-regulation mechanism.

routes.title: Measure the calcifying fluid, so a skeleton phenotype can be diagnosed
routes.intervention: Put pH-sensitive dye imaging and microsensors on edited juveniles and read pH, calcium, carbonate and saturation state in the extracellular calcifying medium directly.
routes.predicted_phenotype: A readout, not a coral. It separates 'the pH pump failed' from 'the organic matrix failed', which no amount of looking at a deformed skeleton can do.
routes.mechanism: Live-tissue measurement under the calicoblastic epithelium.

evidence.cite: Venn et al. 2011, PLoS One 6:e20013 — extracellular pH under the calicoblastic epithelium higher than seawater by about 0.5 pH units in light and 0.2 in dark, in S. pistillata; intracellular pH stable.

Sevilgen et al. 2019, Sci Adv 5:eaau7447 — microsensors and SNARF-1 dye agreed at the same time and place; all parameters elevated relative to seawater. THE ABSTRACT GIVES NO NUMBERS and the paper was not obtained, so no saturation-state value is quoted from it anywhere here.

Ross et al. 2017, Sci Rep 7:14066 — boron-isotope proxy: calcifying fluid pH 8.38 in summer to 8.60 in winter, dissolved inorganic carbon 1.5-2x seawater, saturation about 4x seawater. Proxy-based and from the skeleton, so NOT directly comparable with the dye numbers above; the methods disagree and are not averaged.

routes.evidence_transfer_note: Three genera, three methods, and the methods disagree on absolute values. The route is the measurement, so the transfer question is about whether the TECHNIQUE moves, not the number.

routes.title: Give up the skeleton — the route that works and is still a failure
routes.intervention: Maintain corals as skeleton-free polyps under acidified conditions.
routes.predicted_phenotype: Polyps that live, feed and reproduce with no skeleton at all, and rebuild one when returned to normal conditions. And no reef: no structure, no refuge, no habitat, nothing that makes a coral reef worth having. Included because it draws the line between keeping the animal alive and keeping the ecosystem.
routes.mechanism: Fine & Tchernov's 'physiological refugia': some scleractinians can alternate between soft-bodied and skeletal forms.
routes.lethality_risk: low for the polyp, total for reef function

evidence.cite: Fine & Tchernov 2007, Science 315:1811 — skeleton-producing corals in acidified conditions sustained basic life functions including reproduction 'in a sea anemone-like form' and resumed skeleton building on return. The abstract names no species; duration and survival criteria were not read.

Stanley Jr., Science 317:1032 (2007), a Letter, and the Fine & Tchernov Reply. Read only through a web summary; the PMID is unknown and PubMed returned 0 hits for it under three query shapes while the ORIGINAL paper was found, which is the positive control. Stanley is largely supportive but doubts the two Mediterranean species generalise to zooxanthellate reef-builders; the authors concede they chose slow-calcifying species and write that even if corals survive acidification, reefs will not.

routes.evidence_transfer_label: a stony coral that does not build reefs
routes.evidence_transfer_note: This is the published objection, not ours: the commenter's criticism is precisely that the two slow-calcifying Mediterranean species 'may not be representative' of zooxanthellate reef-builders, and the authors concede they chose slow calcifiers.

routes.title: Give it Durusdinium trenchii: about +1 to 2 degC, and a visibly smaller coral
routes.intervention: Bleach recruits or adult fragments chemically or by heat, then re-inoculate with cultured Durusdinium trenchii.
routes.predicted_phenotype: A colony that bleaches at roughly 1 to 2 degC higher — and grows 29% slower in the laboratory and 38% slower in the field, with Caribbean hosts calcifying at 'nearly half' the rate of those holding native symbionts. Juveniles are worse: clade C grows two to three times as fast as D. You get a coral that survives the heatwave and is small when it is over.
routes.mechanism: A thermotolerant symbiont genus with lower photosynthetic carbon assimilation per cell and more host nitrogen retained by the alga; the host transcriptome shifts toward a heat-stress-like state even at control temperature.
routes.reversibility: moderate — reversion toward C-types is plausible and unverified; re-inoculation is possible
routes.lethality_risk: low in itself; the bleaching step carries the risk

evidence.cite: Berkelmans & van Oppen 2006, Proc Biol Sci 273:2305 — adult A. millepora that shifted from type C to D gained 'around 1-1.5 degrees C', by shuffling of types already present, not uptake from outside. The authors add it 'may not be sufficient' over a century.
Jones & Berkelmans 2010, PLoS One 5:e10437 — type D corals grew 29% slower in the laboratory and 38% slower in the field; bleaching itself cut growth by more than half for up to 18 months.
Little, van Oppen & Willis 2004, Science 304:1492 — clade C-infected juveniles grew two to three times as fast as clade D.

Pettay et al. 2015, PNAS 112:7513 — Caribbean invasion by S. trenchii; tolerance of temperatures 1-2 degC higher, calcification 'reduced by nearly half', authors call the new symbioses 'maladapted'. That reading is their inference, not a fitness measurement.

Kemp et al. 2023, Proc Biol Sci 290:20231403 — COUNTER-EVIDENCE: across diverse coral taxa, Cladocopium and Durusdinium colonies showed similar nutrient exchange at ambient and Durusdinium maintained carbon assimilation and transfer under heat. 'This discovery differs from the prevailing notion that these mutualisms inevitably suffer trade-offs.' Nutrient flux is not calcification, so this does not directly contradict Jones & Berkelmans; it is not reconciled by any single experiment.

Sproles et al. 2020, Environ Microbiol 22:3741 — in the ANEMONE Exaiptasia, D. trenchii assimilated significantly less carbon per cell and obtained more host nitrogen than Breviolum minutum. A mechanism, in a different animal.

Cunning et al. 2020, Mol Ecol 29:2940 — in Montastraea cavernosa, symbiont identity explained 2-14% of transcriptional variance across 3 genets, with D. trenchii shifting host expression toward a heat-response state.

routes.evidence_transfer_label: an anemone or Nematostella, not a coral
routes.evidence_transfer_note: The thermal gain and the growth penalty are both from Acropora millepora; the calcification figure is from unnamed Caribbean hosts; the MECHANISM (reduced carbon assimilation per cell) is from an ANEMONE. Three different levels of transfer in one route.

routes.title: Bleach it on purpose so the heat-tolerant symbiont it already has takes over
routes.intervention: Give colonies that already carry background Durusdinium a controlled sub-lethal bleaching and recovery.
routes.predicted_phenotype: Colonies that come back more than 90% D1a — a type not detectable before — with less photodamage and less symbiont loss when re-heated three months later. Whether it lasts beyond three months is NOT KNOWN from anything verified here.
routes.mechanism: Low-abundance heat-tolerant types proliferate when sensitive types are lost. Crucially the direction depends on severity: after SEVERE bleaching, especially in a warm recovery environment, the heat-tolerant proportion rises sharply; after MILD bleaching it tends to DECREASE.
routes.lethality_risk: moderate — you are deliberately bleaching a colony, and growth falls by more than half for up to 18 months afterwards

evidence.cite: Silverstein, Cunning & Baker 2015, Glob Chang Biol 21:236 — M. cavernosa recovered with >90% D1a, not detected before bleaching; on re-exposure to 32 degC for 10 days three months later, less photodamage and less symbiont loss. Horizon tested: three months.

Cunning, Silverstein & Baker 2015, Proc Biol Sci 282:20141725 — THE RECONCILIATION PAPER. In Orbicella faveolata the heat-tolerant proportion 'dramatically increased following severe experimental bleaching, especially in a warmer recovery environment, but tended to decrease if bleaching was less severe', and higher heat-tolerant proportions 'linearly increased bleaching resistance but reduced photochemical efficiency'. The authors describe the literature itself as conflicting and say they help reconcile it. So the disagreement is CONDITIONAL, not open.

Baker et al. 2004, Nature 430:741 — the original correlative claim: unusual thermally tolerant symbionts are much more abundant on reefs severely affected by recent climate change. A spatial correlation; no time course, and the abstract does not distinguish shuffling from switching.

YOU NEED A RESERVOIR TO SHUFFLE TO. Bay et al. 2016, R Soc Open Sci 3:160322, report that a minimum pre-stress Durusdinium-to-Cladocopium ratio of about 0.003 predicted bleaching severity and recovery in Acropora millepora, with Keppel colonies reaching D dominance between September and December 2005 and cumulative mortality of 8%, 40% and 75% in December, January and February. PMID NOT VERIFIED: a PubMed title search returned 0 hits and the PMCID could not be converted, so this was read at web-page level through a summariser and the numbers are SECOND-HAND. Verify the 0.003 in the full text before using it.

McIlroy et al. 2020, ISME J 14:2424 — in CULTURE, competition may drive Cladocopium dominance outside temperature stress and 'ultimately undermine the efficacy of symbiont turnover as an adaptive mechanism'. No host; reversion in corals is not measured here.

Scoped negative: NO verified multi-year Durusdinium-to-Cladocopium reversion time course was found. Searched PubMed with two tools; 'symbiont shuffling coral' returned 43 hits of which 12 PMIDs were returned and their abstracts not read. PMID 41877353 (2026, Glob Chang Biol, 'Persistent Legacy Effects of Marine Heatwaves on Coral Symbioses') is the most likely source and is TITLE ONLY. The classic 'shuffling reverts' literature (Thornhill 2006) was not located and is not asserted in either direction.

routes.evidence_transfer_note: THE ONE THE LEAD CAUGHT. The reconciliation result that makes this route's severity-dependence statement possible — Cunning, Silverstein & Baker 2015 — is in ORBICELLA FAVEOLATA, a massive Caribbean coral. The persistence result is in Montastraea cavernosa, also massive and Caribbean. The degrees-of-tolerance figure is in Acropora millepora, branching and Indo-Pacific. Applying the severity rule to an Acropora route crosses both genus and growth form and an ocean, and nothing read here tests that.

routes.title: Inoculate SS8, the one lab-evolved strain that worked in an adult coral
routes.intervention: Chemically bleach adult fragments and inoculate with Cladocopium proliferum strain SS8, evolved about ten years at 31 degC.
routes.predicted_phenotype: In Galaxea fascicularis: thermotolerance similar to Durusdinium-hosting fragments of the same colony, but FASTER growth than those fragments at ambient, with the strain still present in moderate abundance two years later. And: only two of four coral genotypes took it up at all. Host-genotype compatibility is the gate.
routes.mechanism: Algal pigments involved in photobiology and oxidative stress were the largest contributors to the difference, suggesting increased photoprotection; SS8 also shows a dampened stress response.
routes.difficulty: moderate — a decade of culture, then a genotype-compatibility screen

evidence.cite: Chan et al. 2023, Glob Chang Biol 29:6945 — 'the first laboratory study to show that thermotolerance of adult corals (G. fascicularis) can be enhanced via the uptake of exogenously supplied, heat-evolved symbionts, without a trade-off against growth under ambient temperature'. Note the growth comparator is DURUSDINIUM-hosting fragments, not wild type, and 'without trade-off' is measured only at ambient.

Johnston et al. 2026, New Phytol 251:1755 — SS8 showed a dampened stress response overall where the wild-type parent responded strongly, across in hospite, expelled and cultured contexts. Two strains.

Chan et al. 2025, Environ Microbiol 27:e70011 — in the ANEMONE Exaiptasia diaphana, SS8 was the most thermotolerant of six heat-evolved strains, but the WILD-TYPE parent WT10 was second, and SS5 and SS9 were among the most thermosensitive. Heat evolution does not reliably help; SS8 is a lineage, not a method.

routes.evidence_transfer_label: an anemone or Nematostella, not a coral
routes.evidence_transfer_note: The adult-coral result is in Galaxea fascicularis, which is neither Acropora nor a massive Caribbean coral; the strain-panel comparison that shows heat evolution does NOT reliably help is in an anemone.

routes.title: Screen evolved strains IN THE HOST, because in-vitro tolerance does not transfer
routes.intervention: Evolve many strains at elevated temperature, then test every one inside coral larvae before any is deployed. The screen is the product.
routes.predicted_phenotype: Most of what you evolved will not work. All ten strains expanded their thermal tolerance in vitro; three of ten improved the holobiont. One strain killed its larvae. The headline '3 of 10' is itself soft: the full text shows those three differ significantly from one wild-type strain and show only a trend against the other.
routes.mechanism: Selection acts on the alga outside the host; the benefit in symbiosis is a separate and largely unpredicted property. Reduced ROS secretion alone did not predict thermal tolerance in symbiosis.
routes.reversibility: high — the output is a decision, not a release
routes.lethality_risk: low, except to the larvae in the failing arms
routes.difficulty: moderate; four years of culture in the cited work

evidence.cite: Buerger et al. 2020, Sci Adv 6:eaba2498 — read at FULL TEXT. Stepwise ratchet 27-28-30-31 degC, about 120 asexual generations over four years versus about 225 for wild type at 27 degC. In vitro at 31 degC for three weeks: heat-evolved cell density up about 66%, wild-type down about 79%; wild-type extracellular ROS 13- to 28-fold higher. In hospite: larvae inoculated at about 10,185 +/- 5,103 cells each, 10 weeks at 27 degC, then 31 degC for 7 days. Three strains held or increased symbiont density (about +26%) while wild-type larvae lost about 61% and 30%. CAVEAT FROM THE TEXT: 'no significant differences between larvae inoculated with any of the SS strains and those inoculated with WT2'. No degree-heating-week figure is given and none should be computed: the holding temperature is not stated to be a climatological maximum.

Scharfenstein et al. 2023, Evol Appl 16:1549 — chemical mutagenesis plus 4.6-5 years of thermal selection: all heat-evolved strains had higher photosynthetic efficiency under heat, but growth-rate trade-offs appeared in at least one lineage at BOTH ambient and elevated temperature, with reduced phosphate and nitrate uptake in some. In vitro only, no host. Disagrees in emphasis with the Galaxea result.

species_of_evidence: coral larvae, host species not printed in the text read
routes.evidence_transfer_note: The PMC text export strips italicised species names, so the host species of the Buerger larvae cannot be stated from what was read. Marked cross_genus because it cannot be shown to match any target.

routes.title: Choose the symbiont per host species, because there is no universal best type
routes.intervention: Screen symbiont genus against host species and match them, instead of deploying one 'heat-tolerant' type everywhere.
routes.predicted_phenotype: The right partner for that host — which in Acropora tenuis juveniles is type C1, not D, the opposite of the Acropora millepora answer. Avoids paying Durusdinium's growth cost in hosts where Durusdinium is not even the more tolerant partner.
routes.mechanism: Host-by-symbiont interaction: the ranking of symbiont types reverses between host species and between life stages.

evidence.cite: Abrego et al. 2008, Proc Biol Sci 275:2273 — A. tenuis juveniles showed lower metabolic costs and better tolerance with type C1 than with D under combined heat and light stress. 'Our results challenge speculations that associations with type D are universally most robust to thermal stress.' The same D type does confer higher tolerance in A. millepora, so the conflict is between host species.
Berkelmans & van Oppen 2006 — the A. millepora result it reverses.

LaJeunesse et al. 2018, Curr Biol 28:2570 — the systematic revision: former Symbiodinium 'clades' are genera in Symbiodiniaceae, with formal descriptions for seven, diverging from about 160 Mya. The abstract does not list the genus names; the familiar mapping is background knowledge, not from this source.

routes.evidence_transfer_note: This is the one route whose POINT is that transfer fails: the ranking of symbiont types reverses between two Acropora species.

routes.title: Genetically engineer the alga — the route everyone proposes and nobody has
routes.intervention: Stably transform a Symbiodiniaceae strain, or CRISPR it, with a ROS-handling or heat-protective change.
routes.predicted_phenotype: Not demonstrated. The honest prediction is a culture that does not take up the construct. Standard methods — biolistics, electroporation, silicon carbide whiskers, nuclear and chloroplast targets — failed to confer resistance in the one published attempt read here.
routes.mechanism: Direct editing. A uracil auxotroph exists as a selection tool, which is a prerequisite rather than a transformation.
routes.reversibility: LOW once released — a self-replicating engineered microbe in open water

evidence.cite: Chen et al. 2019, PLoS One 14:e0211936 — 'The genetic intractability of Symbiodinium microadriaticum to standard algal transformation methods'; unable to confer chloramphenicol or atrazine resistance on strain CCMP2467. The authors note 'no study of successfully applied genome editing has been reported in a dinoflagellate despite the first genetic transformation of Symbiodinium being published about 20 years ago'. SCOPE OF THE NEGATIVE: one strain, one species, those methods and constructs. It does not say transformation is impossible and it explicitly acknowledges an older positive report, which was not verified here.

Levin et al. 2017, Front Microbiol 8:1220 — proposes constructs and assesses CRISPR/Cas9 potential from three Symbiodinium genomes; 'genetic transformation of Symbiodinium has seen little success likely due to the large evolutionary divergence'. Proposed, not demonstrated.

Gavin et al. 2026, Protist 180:126148 — 'Genetic modification in dinoflagellate algae: Some successes, many failures'; the ability to carry out genetic modification in dinoflagellates 'is limited'. The abstract does not enumerate which techniques worked and the body was not read, so no list of existing stable transformants is given here.
Ishii et al. 2018, Sci Rep 8:3237 — a URA3 uracil auxotroph that maintains symbiosis with Exaiptasia only in uracil-containing seawater. A selection tool, NOT a transformation.

Scoped negative: PubMed 'Symbiodiniaceae CRISPR' returns 0, 'Symbiodiniaceae transformation' 7, 'Symbiodinium transformation' 17 (first 10 reviewed by title). A PubMed-index statement only: it does not rule out preprints, non-indexed work or full-text mentions.

routes.evidence_transfer_note: Target and evidence are both the alga. The transfer question here is to OTHER STRAINS, not to another host.

routes.title: Feed the coral to offset what the tolerant symbiont stops giving it
routes.intervention: Supply heterotrophic food, or manage nitrogen, in colonies carrying a low-translocation heat-tolerant symbiont.
routes.predicted_phenotype: Intended: near-normal growth at +1 to 2 degC of tolerance. NOT DEMONSTRATED in any coral. The strongest support is indirect: the published bioenergetic model's own abstract states that bleaching in it is 'exacerbated by nutrients and attenuated by feeding'.
routes.mechanism: Replace the photosynthetic carbon the heat-tolerant alga does not translocate with carbon the host eats.

evidence.cite: Sproles et al. 2020, Environ Microbiol 22:3741 — the carbon deficit this route compensates, measured in an anemone.
Cunning et al. 2017, J Theor Biol 431:49 — model abstract: bleaching 'exacerbated by nutrients and attenuated by feeding'. Model, not measurement.
Kemp et al. 2023, Proc Biol Sci 290:20231403 — COUNTER: no ambient nutrient-exchange deficit was seen, which would make this route a solution to a problem that is not there.

routes.evidence_transfer_label: an anemone or Nematostella, not a coral
routes.evidence_transfer_note: The carbon deficit this route compensates was measured in an anemone, and the counter-evidence says the deficit may not exist in corals at all.

routes.title: Restraint: do not release Durusdinium trenchii where it is not native
routes.intervention: None. Explicitly rule out moving heat-tolerant symbiont lineages across ocean basins.
routes.predicted_phenotype: Reefs that do not acquire a low-diversity clonal invader whose spread is associated with calcification reduced by nearly half. The counterfactual is the Caribbean.
routes.mechanism: An Indo-Pacific symbiont established in Caribbean hosts with low clonal diversity and several widespread clones.
routes.reversibility: none — a self-replicating organism in open water cannot be recalled
routes.lethality_risk: low per colony, high per reef

evidence.cite: Pettay et al. 2015, PNAS 112:7513 — 'Microbial invasion of the Caribbean by an Indo-Pacific coral zooxanthella'; calcification reduced by nearly half versus hosts with natives, which the authors read as maladaptive.

routes.evidence_transfer_note: The harm and the target are the same system.

routes.title: Dose a defined bacterial consortium through a heatwave
routes.intervention: Apply a native, culturable Beneficial Microorganisms for Corals consortium by water dosing every three to five days around a thermal event.
routes.predicted_phenotype: In a tank: 100% of fragments survived a 30 degC, 10-day heat treatment against 60% of placebo-treated controls, with stable photosynthetic performance. And the effect stops when dosing stops — the consortium was not detectable at all after the 15-day recovery period.
routes.mechanism: Correlational omics: dimethylsulfoniopropionate degradation patterns, lipid maintenance, and host transcriptional reprogramming of repair, stress and immune genes. Which of these does the work is not established.
routes.reversibility: high — the strains disappear within weeks

evidence.cite: Santoro et al. 2021, Sci Adv 7:eabg3088 — 80 fragments, five 1.3 L aquaria per treatment, 75-day experiment, ramp 0.5 degC/day to 30 degC held 10 days. '40% survival rate increase'. Full text: 'members of the BMC consortium were not detected after the 15-day period', and BMC and placebo communities 'became indiscernible during the recovery period'. Only three strains were confirmed incorporated at all. Host species name was stripped from the extracted text and is not stated here.

Rosado et al. 2019, ISME J 13:921 — Pocillopora damicornis, seven strains, with a Vibrio coralliilyticus co-challenge. Fv/Fm decline over 26 days: Vibrio 54%, control 40%, probiotic 31%, probiotic+Vibrio 20%. NOTE the consortium was added AFTER the pathogen, so part of the effect is pathogen suppression rather than heat tolerance. The authors state it is 'currently not known if the pBMCs colonize the host'.

A SINGLE dose also works, at least once: de Breuyn et al. 2025, ISME Commun 5:ycaf039 report that 'BMC supplementation significantly prevented mortality in [P.] cf. [verrucosa] at 32 degC, contrasting with a 100% mortality observed in the control group' over a 48-hour shock, 12 fragments per species per treatment. The other species tested survived in both arms, so the result rests on one species, and 48 hours is a shock rather than a bleaching season. That it works within two days argues against slow community assembly as the mechanism.

THE DOSING PROBLEM IS THE ENGINEERING PROBLEM, because the inoculants do not persist. Alginate beads release about a million viable cells per hour per 50 mL flask into the third week at both 26 and 32 degC — IN FLASKS, with no coral, no reef and no flow.

Non-target effects are measurable: BMCs applied three times weekly for three months to healthy Red Sea colonies shifted the skin and gut microbiomes of a coral-dwelling damselfish. The direction was judged beneficial BY THE AUTHORS; the point here is that bystanders are affected at all.
Peixoto et al. 2017, Front Microbiol 8:341 — the framework paper that coined BMC. A proposal; the authors themselves write that the mechanisms 'are poorly understood'.

species_of_evidence: a Brazilian Atlantic coral (genus not stated)
routes.evidence_transfer_note: The 40% survival result's host species was stripped from the extracted text and is not stated. Four studies, at least three genera, two oceans.

routes.title: Use dead bacteria — it worked in the water, and releases nothing alive
routes.intervention: Apply heat-killed consortia instead of live cells, in situ.
routes.predicted_phenotype: Maintained photosynthetic efficiency through a 15-day marine heatwave in Acropora cf. valida, where placebo-treated colonies declined significantly. The ecological-release objection to live probiotics does not apply. Fv/Fm, not survival, is what the abstract reports.
routes.mechanism: Unresolved. That heat-killed cells work at all suggests the mechanism is chemical or cell-wall signalling rather than colonisation — which is consistent with live inoculants disappearing within weeks in every study read here.

evidence.cite: Santoro et al. 2026, Cell Rep 45:117839 — the only in-water trial found: 'both live and one of the heat-killed treatments maintained photosynthetic efficiency (Fv/Fm), whereas placebo-treated corals exhibited significant thermal stress-induced decline'. Colony number, temperature and mortality were not read.

routes.evidence_transfer_note: The only in-water trial, and it is in an Acropora — which makes it the best-matched microbiome route for an Acropora-centred page.

routes.title: Transplant the whole microbiome from a heat-tolerant donor
routes.intervention: Homogenise tissue from wild heat-tolerant donors and inoculate conspecific heat-susceptible recipients.
routes.predicted_phenotype: Less bleaching at 34 degC, with 112 (Pocillopora) and 16 (Porites) donor-specific bacterial species detectable in recipients. The cargo is uncontrolled: a tissue homogenate also carries host cells, Symbiodiniaceae and viruses, so the effect cannot be assigned to bacteria.
routes.mechanism: Transfer of donor-associated bacteria, among everything else in the homogenate.
routes.lethality_risk: low to medium — undefined cargo, possible pathogen carryover

evidence.cite: Doering et al. 2021, Microbiome 9:102 — 'Recipients of both coral species bleached at lower rates compared to the control group when exposed to short-term heat stress (34 degC)'. The authors call for 'field-based long-term studies testing the persistence of the effect'. Colony counts, effect sizes and exposure duration were not read.

routes.evidence_transfer_note: Two genera, both conspecific donor-to-recipient within the study, so the transfer question is to a THIRD genus.

routes.title: Amoxicillin paste on disease lesions — the one that is actually deployed
routes.intervention: Apply amoxicillin in a CoreRx Base 2B paste directly to stony coral tissue loss disease lesions on wild colonies.
routes.predicted_phenotype: Lesions arrested on 70% to 95% of treated lesions in the water, across five species, where the paste alone achieved 4% and 9% — no better than untreated. And the colony keeps developing NEW lesions elsewhere, so this treats lesions, not corals.
routes.mechanism: Kills a bacterial pathogen, or the bacteria associated with one. The pathogen of this disease is unknown, so an antibiotic that works is an empirical fact rather than a mechanism.
routes.reversibility: low to medium — antibiotic released onto a reef
routes.lethality_risk: low to the colony; resistance risk unquantified
routes.difficulty: high — this is diver time, per lesion, indefinitely

evidence.cite: Neely et al. 2020, PeerJ 8:e9289 — 'The effectiveness of the pastes without antibiotics (placebo treatments) was 4% and 9%, no different from untreated controls. Adding amoxicillin to both pastes significantly increased effectiveness to 70% and 84%.' Per species 67% to 90%. A placebo arm in the field, which is rare in this literature.

Shilling, Combs & Voss 2021, Sci Rep 11:8566 — 95% success at healing individual lesions on Montastraea cavernosa over 11 months, but it 'did not necessarily prevent treated colonies from developing new lesions over time'. Chlorinated epoxy was no better than untreated control.

Becker et al. 2026, ISME Commun 6:ycag278 — 41 colonies fate-tracked for 4-5 years: 'Despite repeated antibiotic treatments on some colonies, there was no effect on the diversity of beta-lactamases'. A NEGATIVE OF LIMITED SCOPE: one species, 41 colonies, metagenomic beta-lactamase diversity only. It is not a survey of resistance on the surrounding reef.
Sharp et al. 2020 — 'The pathogen is unknown.'
Scoped negative: statewide Florida deployment totals — how many colonies have been treated — were NOT retrieved from any source read.

routes.evidence_transfer_note: Disease, treatment and target are the same system, which is why this is the one microbial route with a real field record.

routes.title: Phage, given before or within a day of infection — and useless after two
routes.intervention: Introduce a lytic phage against a named bacterial coral pathogen at or within one day of exposure.
routes.predicted_phenotype: Corals that escape white-plague-like infection and do not transmit it, with phage persisting 37 days at about 10^4 per square centimetre of coral surface. Given two days after infection it failed. The therapeutic window is the result.
routes.mechanism: Pathogen-specific lysis.
routes.reversibility: LOW — a self-replicating agent released into water
routes.lethality_risk: low to medium; ecological release is the real risk

evidence.cite: Efrony, Atad & Rosenberg 2009, Curr Microbiol 58:139 — phage BA3 against Thalassomonas loyana; 'successful when the phage was added at the same time as the pathogen or 1 day later, but failed to protect the coral when added 2 days after bacterial infection'. Aquarium; coral species and replicate number not in the abstract.

Scoped negative: no phage work against stony coral tissue loss disease was located. One PubMed query on Thalassomonas/Vibrio phage returned only this paper. 'Not found by one query', not 'does not exist'.

species_of_evidence: coral species not stated in the abstract
routes.evidence_transfer_note: Neither the coral species nor the replicate number is in the abstract, and the pathogen is one named bacterium that is NOT the stony coral tissue loss disease agent.

routes.title: Change the water, not the genome: grow it in the flow you want the shape for
routes.intervention: Grow or place clonal fragments under a chosen flow regime — roughly 1 cm/s against roughly 15 cm/s in the published flume range.
routes.predicted_phenotype: Thin, widely spaced, more symmetric branches in slow flow; more compact, thicker-branched, upstream-biased colonies in faster flow. No genetic change, and the skeleton already laid down does not move — only new growth re-steers.
routes.mechanism: Mass-transfer-limited uptake feeding accretive growth: the balance of advection to diffusion sets how strongly tips out-compete the rest of the surface.

evidence.cite: Chindapol et al. 2013, PLoS Comput Biol 9:e1002849 — read at FULL TEXT. Accretive growth coupled to Navier-Stokes and advection-diffusion, validated against CT scans of Pocillopora verrucosa grown in a flume. Degree of symmetry falls and compactness rises with Peclet number, in both simulated and real colonies. NOTE the paper contradicts itself on the flume speeds: the text says 1e-2 cm/s reduced and 15 cm/s enhanced, the figure caption says about 1 cm/s and 15-20 cm/s. Order of magnitude only.

Paz-Garcia et al. 2015, Oecologia 178:207 — three Pocillopora morphospecies of one mtDNA type across contrasting flow sites; morphology more similar among species under high flow. Confounded by site and species, and no flow speeds in the abstract.

Merks et al. 2003, J Theor Biol 224:153 — COUNTER-EVIDENCE: 'We did not find an effect of flow', and the earlier computational evidence that hydrodynamics changes compactness in laminar flow 'may not be conclusive'. The flow question is genuinely split between modelling groups and is not reconciled here.

Todd 2008, Biol Rev 83:315 — of 1,314 extant species, fewer than 20 have been tested for plasticity; light and water movement are the most important inducers, and adaptiveness is 'yet to be tested rigorously'.

routes.evidence_transfer_note: Every flow result here is Pocillopora. Applying it to Acropora, whose branching architecture is different, is untested.

routes.title: Shade it into a plate
routes.intervention: Shade clonal colonies by roughly 70%, or place them deep or on an inclined surface.
routes.predicted_phenotype: Flatter, laminar or foliose plates instead of digitate or corymbose mounds, with lower surface complexity. The strongest direct evidence is a one-year clonal experiment in ONE genus and it is a PREPRINT, not peer-reviewed.
routes.mechanism: Photoacclimation: trading biomass per unit area against light interception per unit area.

evidence.cite: Ducret et al. 2025, bioRxiv — NOT PEER-REVIEWED. Montipora capitata, 9 genotypes x 6 fragments, 3 shaded (73% light reduction) and 3 control for one year: shaded corals planar/laminar/foliose, controls digitate/corymbose with higher surface complexity, with no significant symbiont-community change. Read at abstract level via a search tool.
Lopez-Londono et al. 2024, PLoS One 19:e0295283 — raising surface inclination reduced light availability by an order of magnitude and triggered photoacclimation like that along depth.

Lesser et al. 2021 — COUNTER: hemispherical colonies fix more carbon at all depths than plating or branching forms, yet plating dominates deeper reefs. So light geometry alone does NOT explain depth zonation, and this route's mechanism is incomplete. Not in PubMed by my search; abstract level only.

Scoped negative: NO published irradiance threshold (in micromoles of photons per square metre per second) tied to a specific morphometric change was found. The 73% reduction above is a single point, not a dose-response.

routes.evidence_transfer_note: One genus, one experiment, and it is a PREPRINT. The strongest direct light-to-plate evidence in this table is also the least peer-reviewed.

routes.title: Pick a shape that does not snap: massive and encrusting over tabular
routes.intervention: Select or steer toward low-colony-shape-factor massive, hemispherical or encrusting forms rather than tabular and arborescent ones.
routes.predicted_phenotype: Lower bending stress at the base and lower dislodgement rates, with a flatter size-mortality curve. Species that become more vulnerable as they grow have bathtub-shaped mortality; mechanically stable ones get safer with size. The bleaching benefit of the same choice is CONTESTED.
routes.mechanism: Smaller projected area perpendicular to flow means a smaller cantilever bending moment at the base per unit of substrate tenacity.
routes.difficulty: moderate — shape control plus species choice

evidence.cite: Madin et al. 2014, Ecol Lett 17:1008 — read at partial FULL TEXT (equation images did not render). Size-dependent mortality is highly consistent within growth form and explained by mechanical vulnerability; 395 colonies for the shape-factor regression, 11 species with about 30 tagged colonies each, Lizard Island. The coefficients are in a supplementary table that was not seen.

Madin & Connolly 2006, Nature 444:477 — model combining wave velocity with beam theory for colonies of any shape, field-tested against change in vulnerability, size and shape with distance from the reef crest.

Loya et al. 2001, Ecol Lett — Sesoko Island 1998, sea temperature peak 2.8 degC above average, species richness down 61% and cover down 85%; finely branched corals most susceptible, massive and encrusting survived. One event, one site. Not found in PubMed by my search.

McCowan et al. 2012 — DISAGREEMENT: across 65 studies, branching, tabular and submassive forms bleach more overall, BUT within families the pattern is inconsistent (branching faviids bleach LESS than massive ones; the reverse in Acroporidae and Poritidae), so growth form is confounded with taxonomy. Burn et al. 2023 add that massive Porites moved from among the LEAST to among the MOST susceptible as bleaching severity rose. 'Branching = loser' is a community-level generalisation with strong taxonomic confounding and severity dependence.

species_of_evidence: 11 species at Lizard Island across five growth forms
routes.evidence_transfer_note: Unusually broad taxonomic coverage for this table — the mechanical result is explicitly ACROSS growth forms, which is what makes it transferable.

routes.title: Pick the opposite shape, because fish live in branches
routes.intervention: Favour branching and corymbose forms where the objective is habitat rather than persistence.
routes.predicted_phenotype: More three-dimensional surface per unit of seabed footprint — measured area exponents of about 2.4 to 2.5 for branching forms against about 1.8 to 2.0 for massive and tabular — and the structural complexity that fish density and biomass track. This route DIRECTLY OPPOSES the storm route above. They cannot both be satisfied by one colony.
routes.mechanism: Structural complexity provides refuge volume at the size classes fish use.
routes.lethality_risk: moderate in storms and heat — see the opposing route

evidence.cite: Chandler et al. 2024, Sci Rep 14:20549 — read at FULL TEXT (table). Underwater photogrammetry, three-dimensional total surface area = a * D^b with D the maximum diameter: Pocillopora 0.709 D^2.50 (n=13, R2 0.95), staghorn Acropora 0.838 D^2.024 (n=14, R2 0.81), table Acropora 2.615 D^1.947 (n=13, R2 0.95), massive Porites 4.58 D^1.836 (n=9, R2 0.75). Single sites, n of 6 to 14, and the paper disagrees with itself on one R2 (table 0.98 against text 0.95).

Graham & Nash, Coral Reefs — strong positive relationship between structural complexity and fish density and biomass. Correlational, and complexity is collinear with coral cover. Not found in PubMed by my search; the publication year (2012 online against 2013 volume) could not be settled.

routes.evidence_transfer_note: Six genera measured by the same photogrammetry method, which is what makes the scaling exponents comparable across growth forms.

routes.title: Simulate the shape before you outplant, using a published growth model
routes.intervention: Run an accretive-growth model over the candidate site's flow and light and predict the colony shape, then choose the site.
routes.predicted_phenotype: A predicted morphospace position — compactness, symmetry, upstream bias — before anything is in the water. The model class is real and runnable; what is MISSING is the mapping from its dimensionless control parameter to a reef flow speed in centimetres per second.
routes.mechanism: Laplacian or advection-diffusion accretive growth, where the resource field the colony absorbs sets where it grows.

evidence.cite: Chindapol et al. 2013 — validated against five real P. verrucosa CT colonies at branch-scale Peclet numbers of 0.016 to 0.288.

Kaandorp & Sloot 2001, J Theor Biol 209:257 — three-dimensional surface-normal accretive growth; with rising Peclet number forms 'gradually transformed from thin-branching ones into more spherical and compact morphologies'. GRADED, not sharp.

Merks et al. 2003, J Theor Biol 224:153 — the explicit curvature rule is NOT needed: 'the model exhibits spontaneous branching, provided that the resource field is computed with enough precision', and compactness depends on the ratio of growth rate to nutrient transport rate.

Merks et al. 2004, J Theor Biol 228:559 — polyp-oriented model: branching arises from a 'polyp fanning effect' on convex surfaces, called a 'more potent branching mechanism than the Laplacian growth mechanism'. Polyp spacing sets branch thickness.

Kaandorp et al. 1996, Phys Rev Lett 77:2328 — morphology 'changes drastically' from diffusion-controlled to hydrodynamically dominated. NOTE: the commonly cited 'Kaandorp 2005 PRL' does not exist; that title belongs to Kaandorp 1999 in Marine Biology.
Scoped negative: NO numeric branching threshold in any dimensionless group was retrieved. Every abstract that comments uses graded language.

routes.evidence_transfer_note: The one calibrated member of this model class was validated against five Pocillopora verrucosa colonies. Nothing validates it for any other genus.

routes.title: Select the cryptic lineage that already has the shape you want
routes.intervention: Choose among sympatric morphs or cryptic lineages whose shape and bleaching threshold differ heritably, rather than trying to induce a shape.
routes.predicted_phenotype: A stable compact or open morph with its associated bleaching threshold, which does not drift back because it is a lineage rather than a plastic response.
routes.mechanism: Some 'morphs' are early cryptic species, not plasticity. Eighteen candidate genes related to skeletal formation were identified in one such pair — and none has been functionally tested.

evidence.cite: Smith et al. 2017, Sci Rep 7:10066 — 'The molecular basis of differential morphology and bleaching thresholds in two morphs of the coral Pocillopora acuta'; two sympatric morphs differ in macro and micro skeletal morphology, with 18 candidate genes and proposed early cryptic speciation.

Hemond, Kaluziak & Vollmer 2014, BMC Genomics 15:1133 — branch tips versus bases in Caribbean Acropora differ in Wnt, Notch and BMP signalling, pH regulation, ion transport and extracellular matrix; 'a relatively small number of genes' may separate staghorn from elkhorn. Correlative expression, no perturbation, species confounded with everything else.

Scoped negative: NO gene knockdown, knockout or transgenic study demonstrating a gene that changes coral colony branching versus plating was found. Two Consensus searches plus PubMed title searches; GWAS, QTL and Acropora hybrid-cross literature were NOT searched, so absence there is not established.

routes.evidence_transfer_note: The morph-with-different-bleaching-threshold result is Pocillopora; the tip-versus-base expression work is Caribbean Acropora.

routes.title: Breed heat-tolerant parents and get about one degree-heating-week per generation
routes.intervention: Select broodstock by measured heat tolerance, cross them, and rear the offspring.
routes.predicted_phenotype: Offspring with measurably higher tolerance — narrow-sense heritability 0.2 to 0.3, and a possible gain of up to 1 degree-heating-week in one generation. Set that against heatwaves that already deliver more than 12 degree-heating-weeks, and against assaying three-to-four-year-old offspring. Worse: selection for short-stress tolerance did NOT improve survival of long stress, with no genetic correlation detected.
routes.mechanism: Additive genetic variance in thermal tolerance.
routes.reversibility: moderate — stock can be culled, released larvae cannot be recalled
routes.difficulty: medium to high — pedigrees over multiple years

evidence.cite: Humanes et al. 2024, Nat Commun — parent selection raised tolerance of 3-4-year-old offspring; narrow-sense h2 0.2-0.3 for both a one-week +3.5 degC and a one-month +2.5 degC simulated heatwave; possible gain up to 1 degree-heating-week in one generation; selection on the short-stress trait did not improve long-stress survival. The authors call the gains moderate and say the result 'demands urgent climate action'.

Lachs et al. 2026, Curr Biol — 'Choice of traits defines the scope for assisted evolution of corals'. A rapid 38.5 degC heat-shock assay was GENETICALLY UNCORRELATED with heatwave bleaching and mortality tolerance, so the assay you choose decides the answer. No genetic trade-offs with reproduction, growth, biomass or symbiont flexibility; weak positive with calcification; and simulations say withstanding future heatwaves 'requires extremely strong selection'.

Quigley, Bay & van Oppen 2020, Mol Ecol — warm-by-cool GBR crosses; heritability high for survival but not growth or bleaching in juveniles, higher at 31 than 27.5 degC, from a limited number of crosses. Also reports that interpopulation breeding INCREASED genetic diversity, which counters the loss-of-local-adaptation objection.

Fuller et al. 2020, Science 369:eaba4674 — the genomic version of this route: chromosome-scale A. millepora assembly, 237 phenotyped whole genomes from 12 GBR reefs with little population structure, balancing selection at a heat-shock co-chaperone (the gene name was stripped from the PubMed text and is not named here), and a GWAS of visual bleaching score on 213 samples feeding a predictive model. THE VARIANCE EXPLAINED IS NOT IN THE ABSTRACT and two attempts at the full text failed, so no R-squared for a coral polygenic score should be quoted from this page. Heat tolerance here is polygenic with weak per-locus effects, which is why the engineerable unit is a score and not a gene.

Bairos-Novak et al. 2021 — the meta-analysis whose headline (high heritability, some above 0.5) sits awkwardly beside the 0.2-0.3 measured directly for heat tolerance. DISAGREEMENT PRESERVED: the trait definition drives the answer, and the meta-analysis itself notes that explicit tests of the heritability of thermal tolerance are lacking.

species_of_evidence: Acropora (species not named in the abstracts read)
routes.evidence_transfer_note: The directly measured heritabilities are Acropora; the meta-analysis spans 19 species and disagrees with them, which is itself a transfer problem.

routes.title: Move warm-adapted parents poleward
routes.intervention: Cross or translocate individuals from warmer, lower-latitude reefs into cooler populations.
routes.predicted_phenotype: Larvae with up to a tenfold increase in the odds of surviving heat stress when a parent comes from a warmer location. At Ningaloo, larvae with ONE warmer-reef parent had 2.2-fold higher survival and those with TWO had 1.6-fold — the one-parent cross beat the two-parent cross, which is not what a simple dose model predicts.
routes.mechanism: Moving standing heritable variation between populations.
routes.lethality_risk: outbreeding depression, disease translocation and loss of local adaptation are the named risks — named by the PROPONENTS of the approach, and not verified in the abstracts read here

evidence.cite: Dixon et al. 2015, Science 348:1460 — 'up-to-10-fold increase in odds of survival of coral larvae under heat stress when their parents come from a warmer lower-latitude location', with heritable expression differences and two genomic regions responding to selection. Larvae under laboratory heat stress; no juvenile or adult field survival, and no test for outbreeding cost. The abstract gives no heritability number.
Kler Lago et al. 2025, Proc Biol Sci — at Ningaloo, one warmer-reef parent gave more than 2.2-fold higher larval survival at 35.5 degC and two parents 1.6-fold, in two species.

Matz et al. 2018, PLoS Genet — MODEL: genomics-derived migration of 0.1-1% immigrants per generation across half the GBR latitudinal range; high migration does not disrupt local thermal adaptation, and standing variation suffices for 20-50 generations (100-250 years) of GRADUAL warming, with rising sensitivity to heatwaves.

routes.evidence_transfer_note: Larval results only. No juvenile or adult field survival in any of them.

routes.title: Cross two Acropora species and hope for heterosis
routes.intervention: Interspecific crosses within Acropora, then rear and test the hybrids.
routes.predicted_phenotype: Sometimes better, sometimes not, and the two studies read here disagree. In one species pair some hybrid groups had higher survival and larger recruits; in another, hybrids did not outperform BOTH purebred parents and the purebred did best. One cross direction failed entirely.
routes.mechanism: Heterosis or novel allele combinations.
routes.reversibility: LOW — novel genotypes capable of introgression
routes.lethality_risk: low per animal; introgression into wild populations is the real irreversibility
routes.difficulty: medium; the cross may work in one direction only

evidence.cite: Chan et al. 2018, Front Mar Sci — two GBR Acropora species pairs, 28 weeks at ambient and elevated temperature and pCO2; 'higher survival and larger recruit size were observed in SOME of the hybrid offspring groups'. Field fitness and backcross potential 'remain to be investigated'. No PMID verified.

Lamb et al. 2024, PeerJ — A. kenti eggs by A. loripes sperm; the reciprocal cross FAILED. Under more than 12 degree-heating-weeks over two months, hybrids 'did not outperform both of their purebred counterparts' and purebred A. loripes did best. Small hybrid sample sizes. DISAGREES with the above. No PMID verified.
Scoped negative: no study of hybrids OUTPLANTED to a reef, or followed through reproduction, was found.

routes.evidence_transfer_note: Within Acropora by construction — the route IS an interspecific cross. The two studies disagree, and they used different species pairs, which may be the whole explanation.

routes.title: Precondition with a sub-bleaching pulse, which nature already does
routes.intervention: Expose colonies to a controlled sub-bleaching thermal trajectory before the main event.
routes.predicted_phenotype: More than 50% less cell mortality and symbiont loss — measured for the NATURAL version of this, in which 75% of past Great Barrier Reef thermal stress events carried such a protective pre-stress trajectory. The warning in the same paper is the point: another 0.5 degC of local warming could abolish the protective trajectory altogether.
routes.mechanism: Acclimatory plasticity, possibly epigenetic.
routes.lethality_risk: low if the pulse is sub-bleaching
routes.difficulty: low in aquaculture, unclear at reef scale; durability unknown

evidence.cite: Ainsworth et al. 2016, Science — 'Climate change disables coral bleaching protection on the Great Barrier Reef'. 75% of past events had a protective pre-stress trajectory cutting cell mortality and symbiont loss by over 50%; +0.5 degC could abolish it. This is the NATURAL phenomenon; no engineered preconditioning regime's durability was found.
Palumbi et al. 2014, Science 344:895 — acclimatisation reached in under two years what selection would take many generations to deliver.
Scoped negative: no durability estimate for an engineered epigenetic priming regime was obtained. PubMed and Consensus queries only.

routes.evidence_transfer_note: The natural protective-trajectory analysis is reef-wide and satellite-based rather than species-specific, which is unusually broad support.

routes.title: Freeze the sperm, because you cannot breed from a genotype that is gone
routes.intervention: Cryopreserve sperm from wild colonies and bank it.
routes.predicted_phenotype: Preserved genotypes and the ability to cross across years and across ranges. It adds NO heat tolerance. In one species frozen sperm fertilised as well as fresh; in another, fertilisation, larval yield, settlement and post-settlement survival were lower by 23%, 23%, 14% and 8%.
routes.mechanism: Vitrification or slow freezing with DMSO.
routes.difficulty: medium, and SEASONAL — banking is restricted to a few spawning nights a year

evidence.cite: Grosso-Becerra et al. 2021, Coral Reefs — Diploria labyrinthiformis sperm viable at least 13 months, motility down about 24%, and fertilisation, larval yield, settlement and post-settlement survival lower by 23%, 23%, 14% and 8% versus fresh. Cryo-recruits survived like controls in the nursery. No PMID verified.
da Cruz 2025 — Mussismilia harttii: 20% DMSO slow freezing, 29.7% motility, 83.6% viability, 100% fertilisation equal to fresh; a repository of 2.4 billion sperm. No PMID verified.

Scoped negative: whole-larva and egg cryopreservation work (Hagedorn and colleagues, cryomesh and laser warming) was NOT retrieved. A PubMed query returned 0 records. Sperm only, in everything read here.

routes.evidence_transfer_note: Both are massive corals, one Caribbean and one Brazilian. The two give DIFFERENT answers on whether frozen sperm matches fresh, and no Acropora figure was retrieved.

routes.title: Put the right crustose coralline alga on the tile
routes.intervention: Condition seeding substrates with strong inducer crustose coralline algae — Titanoderma or Porolithon species — or their extracts.
routes.predicted_phenotype: Far more attached, metamorphosed spat per larva released: Titanoderma cf. tessellatum induced at least 50% settlement in 14 of 15 coral species, mean 81%. But no crustose coralline alga is a universal inducer — three species settled below 10% under every treatment tested — so the alga has to be matched to the coral.
routes.mechanism: Algal chemistry and its associated microbiome, including Pseudoalteromonas and distinct lipid classes, trigger attachment AND metamorphosis together.

evidence.cite: Abdul Wahab et al. 2023, Sci Rep 13:5795 — 15 coral species by 15 GBR crustose coralline algae; Lithophyllaceae best overall; Titanoderma cf. tessellatum at least 50% in 14 of 15 species, mean 81%; algae from a similar light environment to the coral induce more. Laboratory.

Whitman et al. 2020, Sci Rep 10:16397 — live Porolithon onkodes gave over 50% settlement in 9 of 15 species and ethanol extracts in 6 acroporids, but under 10% in Montipora aequituberculata, Mycedium elephantotus and Porites cylindrica under ALL treatments. The authors state it is not a universal inducer.

Jorissen et al. 2021, Sci Rep 11:14610 — all six algae induced settlement of Acropora cytherea but only Titanoderma prototypum promoted settlement ON the alga rather than on nearby dead coral or plastic. Note what this implies: larvae settle on plastic and dead coral in these assays, so a no-cue baseline is NOT zero.

routes.evidence_transfer_note: The 15-by-15 design is the broadest taxonomic coverage of any route here, and its finding is that the pairing MATTERS — three species settled below 10% under every treatment.

routes.title: Tetrabromopyrrole: 100% metamorphosis, 0-2% attachment — a route that fails
routes.intervention: Impregnate surfaces with the bacterial morphogen tetrabromopyrrole.
routes.predicted_phenotype: Larvae that become fully developed polyps within six hours and then do not stick. Attachment of 0 to 2%. This is a wasted cohort, and it is in the table AS A NEGATIVE CONTROL: it shows that metamorphosis and attachment are separable processes and that an assay scoring only metamorphosis will call this a success.
routes.mechanism: The compound triggers metamorphosis without triggering attachment.

evidence.cite: Tebben et al. 2011, PLoS One 6:e19082 — planulae became fully developed polyps within six hours but only a small proportion attached; biofilm density did not change the attached-to-unattached ratio; the compound was found in 4 of 225 isolates.
Siboni et al. 2012, PLoS One 7:e37774 — quantified: metamorphosis 100%, attachment 0-2% in Acropora millepora.

routes.evidence_transfer_note: A negative control, so transfer matters less: the point is that an assay scoring metamorphosis alone will call this a success in any species.

routes.title: Give the spat somewhere to hide: 4 mm grooves
routes.intervention: Seed onto tiles with 4 mm through-grooves and downward-facing surfaces rather than flat tiles.
routes.predicted_phenotype: First-year survival of about 39% against 13% on flat control tiles, in one Acropora tenuis trial. The starkest number in the whole study is not the 39%: it is 100% mortality of recruits on UPPER surfaces, nearly all within six months. Where the spat sits matters more than almost anything else on this list.
routes.mechanism: Refuge from incidental grazing by herbivorous fish and from sediment accumulation.

evidence.cite: Randall et al. 2021, Front Mar Sci — 'Enhancing Coral Survival on Deployment Devices With Microrefugia'; spat survival 2-39% across device types, 100% mortality on upper surfaces, best device (4 mm through-grooves) 39% against 13% for flat control tiles, about half of devices with at least one survivor at one year. No PMID verified; read at search-summary level.

Doropoulos et al. 2017, R Soc Open Sci 4:170082 — settlement three times higher in crevices than on exposed surfaces, but by one month recruit density was similar on both, because crevices carry negative density dependence. The refuge advantage is partly spent by a month.

routes.evidence_transfer_note: One reef, one genus, and the device geometry is probably more transferable than the survival percentage.

routes.title: Wedge unattached tetrapods into the reef instead of gluing anything
routes.intervention: Settle larvae on small concrete tetrapods and wedge them into reef crevices without cement or bolts.
routes.predicted_phenotype: About 9.6% recruit survival at one year with 67% of tetrapods holding at least one colony, at 5 to 18 times lower outplanting cost and 1.5 to 7% of the deployment time. The trade-off is measured: bolting takes about 120 seconds against about 10 for wedging, and it doubled or quadrupled the proportion of units still holding a live coral.
routes.mechanism: Self-wedging geometry plus refuge, with no attachment step.

evidence.cite: Chamberland et al. 2017, Sci Rep 7:18076 — Curacao: average recruit survival 9.6% after one year on concrete tetrapods, 67% of tetrapods with at least one colony, costs 5-18x lower than traditional attached methods, deployment 1.5-7% of the time.

Mendoza Quiroz et al. 2025, Restoration Ecology — bolting ceramic stars took about 120 s against about 10 s for wedging tetrapods, but doubled (D. labyrinthiformis, 8 months) or quadrupled (A. palmata, 6 months) the proportion of units retaining a live coral. Cementing raised retention but not live-coral yield. No PMID verified.

routes.evidence_transfer_note: Caribbean, and the attachment trade-off was measured on one massive and one branching species with different answers (doubled against quadrupled).

routes.title: Release hundreds of thousands of larvae into a netted plot
routes.intervention: Rear larvae ex situ and release 3-4 x 10^5 competent larvae into a mesh-enclosed reef plot for several days.
routes.predicted_phenotype: Colonies on the reef at three years, about 16 cm across, spawning — where control plots produced no visible colonies of that species at all. Now the arithmetic: 47 colonies survived from about 900,000 larvae across three plots, which is about 5 x 10^-5 larvae per surviving colony, at a production cost of USD 35.20 each.
routes.mechanism: Bypasses larval supply limitation at a degraded site.
routes.reversibility: low — released larvae cannot be recalled

evidence.cite: Dela Cruz & Harrison 2020, PLoS One 15:e0242847 — about 300,000 A. loripes larvae per plot, 27.8 +/- 6.7 spat per tile against zero in controls, 47 colonies surviving at 35 months at a mean 7.9 cm diameter, USD 35.20 production cost per surviving colony. The 5e-5 figure is MY ARITHMETIC from those numbers and assumes the 47 is the total across three plots, which the abstract does not state explicitly.

Dela Cruz & Harrison 2017 — survivorship began stabilising after about five months, juveniles visible to the eye at nine months, 2.3 colonies per square metre at three years with a mean 16.1 +/- 0.7 cm diameter, and the colonies spawned at three years. Natural recruitment produced no visible A. tenuis colonies.

routes.evidence_transfer_note: Two Acropora species, one site, two trials by the same group. The 2020 paper's own abstract says only one earlier experiment had demonstrated long-term success.

routes.title: Play reef sound at the settlement site
routes.intervention: Deploy a solar-powered reef soundscape playback system at a seeding site.
routes.predicted_phenotype: About 1.7 to 1.8 times more settlers near the speaker, detectable at least 30 m away, with a maximum of seven times in one trial. The honest frame: in flow-through conditions the response was minimal and the difference BETWEEN TWO REEFS was tenfold, so site choice outweighs the speaker.
routes.mechanism: Larval detection of low-frequency biological reef sound; fish calls below 1 kHz may be detectable hundreds of metres away.

evidence.cite: Aoki et al. 2024, R Soc Open Sci 11:231514 — settlement 1.7x on average (maximum 7x) at enriched sites on a degraded reef, still above control at 30 m or more from the speaker. A brooding coral.
Aoki et al. 2026, Sci Rep — broadcast spawner Diploria labyrinthiformis: 1.79x in static cups, but in flow-through tents the response was minimal and there was a tenfold difference between two reefs.
Aoki et al. 2024, JASA Express Lett 4(10) — the aquarium and field demonstration in Favia fragum.

Scoped negative: every verified acoustic result comes from ONE laboratory group, no independent replication was found, and NO Acropora value exists. Searched PubMed with 'reef sound playback coral larvae settlement' only (8 hits).

routes.evidence_transfer_note: A brooding Caribbean coral and a massive Caribbean broadcast spawner. THERE IS NO ACROPORA VALUE AT ALL, and every verified result comes from one laboratory group with no independent replication found.

routes.title: Screen the site for sediment before you spend anything else
routes.intervention: Pre-screen candidate sites for sediment deposition and substrate stability, and reject the bad ones.
routes.predicted_phenotype: Avoids near-total failure. Two millimetres of sediment cuts settlement probability to 25% or less and four millimetres suppresses it; burying recruits under four millimetres cuts ten-day survival to between 0 and 31%. The field failure case is stark: at one site 9% of ceramic devices held a recruit at 21 months and 0% of travertine tiles did, DESPITE travertine attracting more than 2.5 times the settlement.
routes.mechanism: Burial, abrasion and substrate instability kill recruits regardless of everything upstream.

evidence.cite: Rodriguez-Ruano et al. 2026, Commun Biol 9 — six Caribbean species: 2 mm sediment cut settlement probability to 25% or less, 4 mm suppressed it, and 4 mm burial cut 10-day recruit survival to 0-31%, a 3-25x mortality risk.
