Macroalgae too: Webster et al. 2015, PLoS One 10:e0124162 — at Ningaloo over nine months, settlement on tile undersides was 93% lower and recruit survival 79% lower in caged macroalgae-dense plots, with recruits up to 58% smaller. CONFOUNDED: caging also removes herbivory.

Removing the macroalgae helps for a year and then stops. Smith et al. 2025, J Environ Manage 383:125322: 'Sea-weeding enhances early coral survival on seeding devices, but benefits of seeding diminish after one year'; 1.3 surviving colonies per device at two years, 50% of devices with one live coral, site survival 37-93%, and USD 334-577 per surviving coral. So weeding buys year one at a cost that recurs forever.

DO NOT MODEL HERBIVORY AS MONOTONIC PROTECTION. Penin et al. 2011, Hydrobiologia: excluding predators and grazers did NOT change total mortality of Acropora striata recruits — more than half dead within seven days either way — it changed the CAUSE, from predation (50.0% of dead recruits damaged or missing) to competition with turf algae and sediment (91.7% intact). This disagrees with the caging result above. No PMID verified.

Waters et al. 2025, Restoration Ecology — Lizard Island, 21 months: 9% of ceramic devices had at least one recruit (all unattached) and 0% of travertine tiles did, despite travertine settlement more than 2.5x ceramic. Sand deposition and unconsolidated rubble killed most. No PMID verified. A failure case, kept in deliberately.

routes.evidence_transfer_note: Four studies across two oceans agreeing on direction, which is why this is the best-supported route in the recruitment group.

routes.title: Skip sexual recruitment entirely: microfragment the adults
routes.intervention: Cut massive corals into roughly 1 cm2 microfragments and array them so they fuse.
routes.predicted_phenotype: Up to ten times more tissue than large fragments over 31 months, once plots with heavy predation are excluded — and predation hit the microfragments and not the large ones. This route does not solve the recruitment bottleneck; it goes around it, which means it adds no genetic diversity at all.
routes.mechanism: Injury-driven rapid edge growth, with a possible immune trade-off.

evidence.cite: Page et al. 2018, Ecol Eng — Florida Keys, 31 months: Orbicella faveolata and Montastraea cavernosa microfragments against 16-64 cm2 fragments; survival and growth did not differ, but after excluding plots with more than 40% predation, O. faveolata microfragment arrays produced 10x more tissue. Initial predation hit microfragments only. No PMID verified.

routes.evidence_transfer_note: Target and evidence are both massive Caribbean corals. The route is explicitly FOR slow-growing massive corals, so this is well matched — and it is a reason not to read it across to branching taxa.

routes.title: Put it where it will still be alive in 2050
routes.intervention: Site restoration by projected bleaching risk rather than by access.
routes.predicted_phenotype: Restored colonies that are not sitting in the places most likely to cook. Current practice does the opposite: restoration sites cluster near human settlements, outcomes are not predicted by environmental covariates, most restored localities face high or severe bleaching risk by mid-century, and more than half of recently restored sites are ALREADY affected.
routes.mechanism: Siting. The cheapest intervention on this page and the one least often made.

evidence.cite: Mula et al. 2025, Nat Ecol Evol 9:822 — 'Restoration cannot be scaled up globally to save reefs from loss and degradation'. An erratum exists (PMID 40442326) and was NOT read, so what it corrects is unknown.

routes.evidence_transfer_note: A siting decision, not a biological claim.

routes.title: Get one bred cohort into the water, under permit, and measure it
routes.intervention: A permitted, monitored field trial of selectively bred stock through a real bleaching event.
routes.predicted_phenotype: The first field survival data for bred versus wild corals. NO SUCH TRIAL WAS LOCATED. The programme furthest along chose larval seeding and seeding of aquaculture-propagated corals for its 2025 pilots on technology-readiness grounds; assisted evolution was not among them.
routes.mechanism: Permits, monitoring and readiness gating.
routes.lethality_risk: low per colony; the risks are genetic and regulatory

evidence.cite: Scoped negative: no evidence was found that any assisted-evolution product has been deployed on the Great Barrier Reef. Scope: one web search, two gbrrestoration.org pages (read at page-summary level), plus PubMed and Consensus. The reports index and the programme's own papers were NOT read. Absence of evidence in a limited search.

REGULATION, all UNVERIFIED legal status. Australia's Gene Technology Amendment (2019 Measures No. 1) Regulations reportedly exempt SDN-1 edits (a site-directed nuclease with no repair template) from the definition of a GMO, which would plausibly put a plain CRISPR indel outside GMO law if no editing machinery is inherited. That is an INFERENCE from a search summary, not legal advice: the Schedule 1 wording was not obtained, the legislation.gov.au fetch returned only a table of contents, and a 2025 minor-measures amendment may have changed it. Separately, Marine Park and EPBC approvals would apply to any release whatever the GM status, and neither was read.

VERIFIED by direct fetch: the United States is listed as having signed the Convention on Biological Diversity in 1993 but not ratified it, so it is not a Party; and neither the United States nor Australia appears as a Party to the Cartagena Protocol. The Protocol's transboundary rules would therefore not bind an Australian release of an Australian coral.

routes.evidence_transfer_note: Regulatory and programmatic; no organism-level evidence.

routes.title: Treat every route above as a bridge, and say what it is a bridge to
routes.intervention: Fund the interventions as a portfolio AND cut emissions, rather than treating them as alternatives.
routes.predicted_phenotype: Under moderate warming, reefs that persist. Under high emissions, the same reefs lost anyway. The modelling says adaptation succeeds under lower-emissions scenarios and fails under higher ones, and transplanting tolerant individuals at 1-5% per year speeds adaptation without changing which side of that line you are on.
routes.mechanism: Buying time. Berkelmans and van Oppen's own phrase for the symbiont route is that it may be enough to 'buy time while greenhouse reduction measures are put in place'.

evidence.cite: Bay et al. 2017, Sci Adv — genomic models: adaptation succeeds under RCP2.6 and RCP4.5 and fails under RCP6.0 and RCP8.5; transplanting tolerant individuals at 1-5% per year speeds adaptation.

Bostrom-Einarsson et al. 2020, PLoS One — 60% of restoration projects monitored for under 18 months, MEDIAN RESTORED AREA 100 SQUARE METRES, 229 species in 72 genera, 59% of studies on fast-growing branching corals, reported survival 60-70%. The authors list absent objectives, non-standard monitoring and poorly designed projects, and say restoration is not a replacement for climate action.

Bayraktarov et al. 2016, Ecol Appl — 235 studies, 954 observations; median reported cost about USD 80,000 per hectare in 2010 dollars, mean about USD 1.6M, true median likely 2-4x higher, with coral reefs among the most expensive habitats and median coral survival 64.5%, mostly assessed over one to two years, with publication bias toward success.

van Oppen et al. 2017, Glob Chang Biol 23:3437 — the framing paper, naming selective breeding, assisted gene flow, conditioning and microbiome manipulation, and proposing a decision tree and consideration of alternative or hybrid ecosystem states.

DISAGREEMENT PRESERVED. Against: Hughes et al. 2023 argue rehabilitation may be feasible only for very small areas of high economic value and that more ambitious outcomes 'remain elusive and may even be counter-productive'. For: Anthony et al. 2020 argue interventions are needed whatever the emissions trajectory, as a portfolio. Lockie 2025 argues the critics show 'singular voices, polemic arguments, empirical short-cuts, and premature closure' — which is a social-science critique OF THE CRITICS and is itself one side. None has a verified PMID here.

routes.evidence_transfer_note: Programme-level. The underlying models are Acropora-parameterised, which is noted inside the route.

recommendation.why_two_fields: Because the honest answer to 'what should we do' and the honest answer to 'what should we BUILD' are different routes, and collapsing them into one field would misrepresent both. The first is siting, which is cheap, reversible and boring. The second is symbiont shuffling. The two sections below say so in that order.
recommendation.If you only get to do one thing: Pick the reef, not the coral. Mula et al. 2025 found that restoration sites cluster near human settlements, that outcomes are not predicted by environmental covariates, and that most restored localities face high or severe bleaching risk by mid-century with more than half already affected. Nothing else on this page changes the answer by as much, costs as little, or is as reversible. It is also the least interesting thing to publish, which is probably why the siting data look the way they do.
recommendation.If you have to engineer something:
Symbiont shuffling by controlled sub-lethal bleaching, in colonies already carrying a background heat-tolerant type. It is the only route on this page with a causal field-scale coral phenotype attached to a number of degrees (about +1 to 1.5 degC, Berkelmans & van Oppen 2006), it needs no genetic modification and therefore probably no GMO regulator, it requires nothing to be cultured or released, and it is partly reversible. It is chosen over Durusdinium INOCULATION, which gets the same tolerance, because inoculation with a non-native lineage is irreversible in open water and the Caribbean shows what that looks like: a clonal invader associated with calcification reduced by nearly half.

The reasons not to do it are stated plainly. You are deliberately bleaching a living colony; growth falls by more than half for up to 18 months afterwards. You need a pre-existing reservoir of the tolerant type or there is nothing to shuffle to. Durability is verified for THREE MONTHS and no longer. And the direction is conditional: after SEVERE bleaching in a warm recovery environment the tolerant proportion rises sharply, but after MILD bleaching it tends to DECREASE — so an intervention that is too gentle does the opposite of what you wanted.
recommendation.The single most useful experiment nobody:
Cross a symbiont intervention with a host trait in one factorial design and measure both the thermal threshold AND the growth rate at ambient. Every thermal route on this page has been tested alone. No study read here crosses them, so whether two interventions add, interact or cancel is unknown in corals — our own simulation says additive, and that is a statement about a four-parameter box in one model, not about a coral.

The second most useful: a multi-year time course of a shuffled symbiont community. The three-month persistence result is the longest verified horizon for shuffling anywhere in the sources read, and a route whose durability is unknown past one season is being discussed as though it were a decade.
recommendation.What we would NOT do:
Engineer the animal, for now. CRISPR works in Acropora millepora — that is real and recent. Counted from the sources read here, SIX genes have been targeted in a reef-building coral: FGF1a, GFP and RFP (Cleves et al. 2018, chosen to show the method works), HSF1 (Cleves et al. 2020), SLC4-gamma (Tinoco et al. 2023) and SLC26A11 (Maruyama et al. 2026, reported in Aiptasia and in a reef-building coral). Only the last three carry an informative trait phenotype, and every one of the six is in the INJECTED GENERATION. There is no stable germline coral line anywhere in this literature, Acropora takes years to reach reproductive size, spawning is seasonal, and editing adult colonies has not been shown. The two coral gene edits with heat or skeleton phenotypes are both LOSS of function: knocking out HSF1 makes a coral worse, and knocking out SLC4-gamma breaks its skeleton. Neither tells you how to make one better. The animal-engineering route is where the science is most exciting and the design leverage is currently lowest.

We would also not deploy a transgenic symbiont. Not on principle — because no one has made one. Standard transformation methods failed on the one strain where the attempt was published, and the PubMed index returns zero for Symbiodiniaceae CRISPR. And unlike an edited coral, an engineered alga is a self-replicating microorganism in open water: the one route here whose irreversibility is categorical rather than practical.
recommendation.The thing the question gets wrong: 'Could you engineer a coral' treats thermal tolerance as the specification. The literature says the binding constraint is somewhere else. Adult corals are not generally what fails first in restoration — recruitment is. First-year survival of settlers spreads over more than tenfold across sites, devices and thermal years (9.6% on tetrapods in Curacao; 2 to 39% across device types in one Acropora tenuis trial; 33% against 2% between a normal and a heatwave year in Moorea; effectively zero yield at 21 months at one Lizard Island site). In the best-documented larval seeding experiment, 47 colonies survived from roughly 900,000 larvae. A heat-tolerant coral that cannot recruit is a heat-tolerant coral you have to keep planting by hand.
recommendation.The arithmetic nobody puts on the slide: The median coral restoration project covers 100 square metres (Bostrom-Einarsson et al. 2020, from a review of the field). The Great Barrier Reef Marine Park is about 344,400 square kilometres. Covering even one square kilometre at the median project size takes ten thousand projects. Reef habitat area is far smaller than Marine Park area, so that ratio overstates the gap — but not by the four orders of magnitude it would need to close. Reported restoration costs run about USD 80,000 per hectare at the median in 2010 dollars, with the true median likely two to four times higher and coral reefs among the most expensive habitats to restore. Every route on this page should be read against that denominator.
recommendation.What would change our mind: A verified multi-year field time course showing a shuffled or inoculated symbiont community holding, with growth measured and not just survival, would move the symbiont route from 'buys a season' to 'buys a decade'. A stable germline coral line would move the gene scale from a calibration tool to a design surface. And a single cross-factorial experiment showing that two interventions combine super-additively would change the recommendation from 'pick one' to 'stack them'.

recommendation_title: If you asked us to actually do it

judge_gene_candidates.what_it_would_actually_produce: Larvae that die rapidly at 34 degC and are fine at 27 degC. This is the gene that has a published coral heat phenotype, and the phenotype is WORSE, not better. Removing it removes the heat-shock response; nothing shows that adding more of it adds tolerance.
judge_gene_candidates.distinguishing_question: Are you describing a loss-of-function result? If the answer is 'they knocked it out and the coral died in the heat', this is the paper and it is not a route to a better coral.

judge_gene_candidates.what_it_would_actually_produce: A coral with a defective skeleton, with severity tracking the mutation frequency. It is a skeleton gene, not a heat gene, and it arose by duplication at the origin of stony corals.
judge_gene_candidates.distinguishing_question: Is the phenotype about the SKELETON or about BLEACHING? If skeleton, it is almost certainly this one, and almost certainly in the losing direction.

judge_gene_candidates.species_of_evidence: Exaiptasia and, per the same abstract, a reef-building coral
judge_gene_candidates.what_it_would_actually_produce: Reduced symbiosis — the coral loses the alga. The paper's frame is the evolutionary co-option of lysosomal machinery for photosymbiosis.
judge_gene_candidates.distinguishing_question: Does the claimed gene affect the SYMBIOSIS itself rather than the host's stress response? Then it is this one, and the phenotype is the thing every other route is trying to prevent.

judge_gene_candidates.gene: An unnamed heat-shock co-chaperone under long-term balancing selection
judge_gene_candidates.species_of_evidence: Acropora millepora, 237 whole genomes across 12 GBR reefs
judge_gene_candidates.what_it_would_actually_produce: Nothing, on its own. This is a population-genomic signature, not a perturbation. NOTE: the gene's NAME was stripped from the PubMed text we read, so we cannot tell you what it is called, and neither could anyone working from the abstract alone. Heat tolerance in this species is polygenic with weak per-locus effects.
judge_gene_candidates.distinguishing_question: Did they EDIT it, or did they find it in a genome scan? If the evidence is 'this locus is under selection' or 'this locus came up in a GWAS', there is no demonstrated phenotype behind it.

judge_gene_candidates.what_it_would_actually_produce: It was a METHOD-DEVELOPMENT target, chosen alongside GFP and RFP to show that Cas9 ribonucleoprotein injection works in coral eggs at about 50% mutation frequency. No heat or skeleton phenotype is claimed for it.
judge_gene_candidates.distinguishing_question: Is the paper from 2018 and about whether CRISPR works in coral at all? Then the gene is incidental.

judge_gene_candidates.gene: Eighteen candidate skeletal-formation genes in Pocillopora acuta
judge_gene_candidates.species_of_evidence: two sympatric morphs of P. acuta
judge_gene_candidates.what_it_would_actually_produce: Unknown. These are candidates from population genomics that distinguish two morphs differing in skeletal morphology AND bleaching threshold. None has been functionally tested, and the authors' own reading is that the morphs may be early cryptic species — so the 'gene for it' may really be 'a different species'.
judge_gene_candidates.distinguishing_question: Does the claim involve colony SHAPE? No gene has ever been shown to change coral branching versus plating by perturbation, in any species.

judge_gene_candidates.gene: Wnt, Notch and BMP pathway members enriched at branch tips
judge_gene_candidates.species_of_evidence: Acropora cervicornis and A. palmata, tip versus base RNA-seq
judge_gene_candidates.what_it_would_actually_produce: Unknown. Differential expression between the tip and the base of a branch, with the authors suggesting 'a relatively small number of genes' may separate staghorn from elkhorn form. Correlative, no perturbation, and the two species differ in everything else as well.
judge_gene_candidates.distinguishing_question: Is the evidence an expression difference between two parts of the same colony? That is a correlate of growth, not a control knob for it.

gene_table_title: “They said they found a gene for it” — what that could mean
gene_table_note: Several genes fit that description and they do not produce the same animal. Six genes have been targeted by CRISPR in a reef-building coral in the sources read here, and only three of those carry an informative trait phenotype; the rest were chosen to demonstrate that the method works at all. Every one is in the injected generation. The last column is the question that would tell them apart.

welfare.Is a coral a welfare subject?: Scleractinian corals are cnidarians: a nerve net, no brain, no centralised nervous system. The usual sentience arguments for vertebrates and cephalopods do not transfer, and no regulator we could identify treats coral research as animal research. We are not going to claim a settled answer from a literature search that did not address the question.
welfare.What the real objection is: It is ecological, not individual. Almost every route here acts on a POPULATION or an ECOSYSTEM, and several release a self-replicating organism into open water. A transgenic symbiont, a therapeutic phage and an amoxicillin paste are not recallable in the way a laboratory animal is, and the harm, if there is one, lands on an ecosystem that nobody owns.
welfare.The one documented harm in this table: Durusdinium trenchii established in Caribbean hosts, where it is not native, with low clonal diversity and calcification in affected hosts 'reduced by nearly half' relative to hosts carrying native symbionts (Pettay et al. 2015). The authors read the new symbioses as maladapted. That is an inference rather than a fitness measurement, and it is the clearest instance on this page of a heat-tolerance gain arriving with an ecosystem-scale cost.
welfare.Deliberate harm as a method: Two routes here work by injuring the coral on purpose. Symbiont shuffling requires deliberately bleaching a living colony, after which growth falls by more than half for up to 18 months. Microfragmentation works BECAUSE of injury-driven edge growth. Both are standard practice and neither is usually described this way.
welfare.Antibiotic release: Amoxicillin paste is applied directly onto wild reefs, lesion by lesion, for a disease whose pathogen is unknown. One metagenomic study of 41 colonies found no effect on beta-lactamase diversity after repeated treatment. That is a narrow negative — one species, 41 colonies, one gene family — and not a survey of resistance on the surrounding reef, which nobody read here has done.
welfare.The honest asymmetry: The counterfactual is not an undisturbed reef. It is a reef that in many places is already losing most of its coral, and a median restoration project that covers 100 square metres. Precaution about intervention has to be weighed against a baseline that is itself moving fast, and the people arguing both sides of that agree on the numbers and disagree about what follows.

welfare_title: Welfare, ecological risk and what is actually at stake
limitations: NONE OF THESE ROUTES HAS BEEN ATTEMPTED HERE. This is a reading of a literature, with two simulations beside it. No coral was touched.

Every PMID cited has been title-matched in PubMed, but READ LEVELS VARY and are given per source. Most are abstract-level. Three papers were read at full text (Buerger 2020, Chindapol 2013, Chandler 2024, and parts of Santoro 2021, Rosado 2019 and Madin 2014). An abstract-level claim is not a reading of a paper, and methods details, sample sizes and effect sizes that live in full texts are mostly absent here.

Routes carrying evidence with no PMID are marked. Several real and relevant studies are not indexed in PubMed, or were not found there: Kaandorp 1999, Loya et al. 2001, Doropoulos 2015/2016, Penin et al. 2011, Randall et al. 2021, Chan et al. 2018, Lamb et al. 2024, Page et al. 2018, the cryopreservation papers and the Fine & Tchernov comment and reply. Their claims are carried at search-summary level and should not be treated as equal to the PMID-verified rows.

The evidence_strength labels are OURS. They compress a judgement about what a study shows into one token, and two people could label the same paper differently. The evidence list under each route is the thing to read.
Reversibility, lethality risk and difficulty are UNQUANTIFIED JUDGEMENTS, not measurements. No route has a measured probability of anything attached to those three fields.

This table under-represents what has been tried and failed, because failures are published less. The one systematic review here notes publication bias toward success in the restoration-cost literature, and the two deliberate failure cases we did keep (tetrabromopyrrole, and the Lizard Island device trial) are in because they happened to be published, not because we searched for failures.

Several of the negatives are scoped to a single PubMed query shape and say so inline. 'Not found by this search' is not 'does not exist', and preprints, non-indexed journals, datasets and theses were largely not searched.

Regulatory statements are the weakest content on this page. No primary legal text was read. The Convention on Biological Diversity and Cartagena Protocol party statuses were verified by fetching the treaty pages; everything about Australian gene-technology law, Marine Park permits, the US Endangered Species Act and FDA jurisdiction is a search summary or an inference, and is labelled as such in the route.

The outcome classes are regex tags over our own prose, so they describe how we wrote a route as much as what the route does. The ordering rule is declared with them because getting it backwards would silently retag most of the table.

provenance.pmid_policy: Every PMID in this file is in a verified set drawn from the research blocks, each of which records the identifier as fetched and title-matched with PubMed's get_article_metadata. build_routes.py refuses to write the file if any cited PMID falls outside that set, so an invented identifier cannot reach it. Twelve were additionally re-fetched directly in this session and their titles re-checked; those carry pmid_reverified_here and a DOI.

evidence_transfer.rule: Where a route's evidence spans several taxa, the WEAKEST applicable transfer is recorded, because that is the assumption the route actually rests on.
evidence_transfer.why_this_exists: The symbiont-shuffling route leans on Cunning, Silverstein & Baker 2015, which is in ORBICELLA FAVEOLATA — a massive Caribbean coral — while the CRISPR precedent, the assisted-evolution programme and most of the morphology work are Acropora-centred. Transfer between them is an assumption, and before this field existed it was invisible on the page.
